tests.covers_criterion: ParseAmount with more than two decimals ("1.234") returns a non-nil error. (TestParseAmountRejectsMoreThanTwoDecimalsCDR0002)
ParseLine returns an error when the amount field is invalid. (TestParseLineInvalidAmountCDR0002)

result.notes: All tests are in parse/parse_cdr0002_test.go. I did not run them because I only have file tools here. The outcomes below come from reading parse/parse.go. Five tests should fail on the current code because ParseAmount ignores the errors from strconv.ParseInt and quietly cuts the fraction to two digits: Letters, TrailingGarbage, Empty, MoreThanTwoDecimals and ParseLineInvalidAmount. TestParseAmountValidValuesCDR0002 is the exception. It checks the constraint that valid values keep their current results, so it should pass on the current code and must keep passing after the fix. The existing parse/parse_test.go expects "7" -> 700, "-1.50" -> -150 and ParseLine("acct , 3.25") -> 325. Keep accepting leading and trailing whitespace (TrimSpace), one optional leading '-', and one or two decimals; a trailing zero like "1.50" must still parse. ParseLine("acct,") has an empty amount field and must return an error. Do not change the ParseAmount or ParseLine signatures.

result.summary: I changed parse.ParseAmount in parse/parse.go so it rejects invalid amounts instead of returning a wrong value with a nil error. I did not run the tests (no shell tool in this role); the reasoning below is from reading the code against parse/parse_cdr0002_test.go and parse/parse_test.go. After trimming spaces and an optional leading '-', the amount must be digits, optionally followed by '.' and one or two digits. Anything else returns an error: empty input, letters, trailing junk like "12.3x", a lone "-", "12." or "1.234". The strconv.ParseInt error is no longer ignored, and amounts too large to hold in cents now return an out-of-range error. Valid values are unchanged: "12.34" gives 1234, "-5" gives -500, "0.5" gives 50 and "-1.50" gives -150. Neither signature changed. ParseLine already returned ParseAmount's error, so it now fails on bad amounts without any edit. A small helper, isDigits, was added.
assumptions: Spaces around the amount are still trimmed as before, so ParseLine("acct , 3.25") in the existing test still parses.
Trailing dots ("12."), leading dots (".5"), a '+' sign and a lone "-" are invalid because they do not match [-]digits[.digits].
risks: Callers that relied on the old lenient parsing (".5", "12." or garbage turning into 0) now get errors.
Error messages are new text and not sentinel errors, so callers can't match on a specific error with errors.Is.

findings.requirement: Overflow/range check in ParseAmount (math import, `w > (math.MaxInt64-99)/100`, 'out of range' error)
findings.description: The intent only asks for errors on empty input and on anything that is not [-]digits[.digits] with at most two decimals. The added range check rejects syntactically valid amounts that are too large. No acceptance criterion needs it. It is a small, defensible hardening, but it is behavior the intent did not request. A human may want to confirm it is wanted.
findings.evidence: parse/parse.go diff: `if err != nil || w > (math.MaxInt64-99)/100 { return 0, fmt.Errorf("parse: amount %q out of range", orig) }` and the new `math` import.
